questions.title: One zero versus two
questions.body: For product-except-self without division, what is the output for `[2,0,4,0]`?
questions.explanation: Every exclusion still leaves at least one zero. Prefix/suffix products handle this without division; a one-zero special case cannot be reused for two zeros.

questions.title: Prefix observation
questions.body: Pseudocode: `p=1; for i=0..3: ans[i]=p; p*=a[i]`, with a=[2,3,4,5]. What is ans before the suffix pass?
questions.explanation: Write the prefix before multiplying the current element. Each position then excludes itself on the left; the suffix pass supplies its right product.

questions.title: Space accounting
questions.body: A Θ(n) product-except-self algorithm stores prefixes in the returned n-element vector and uses two scalar accumulators. Ignoring output storage, what is auxiliary space?
questions.explanation: The required output uses Θ(n) storage but is explicitly excluded here. Count any extra prefix/suffix arrays if the implementation allocates them.

questions.title: A bound is not a case name
questions.body: A worst-case runtime is T(n)=3n+7. Which statement is correct?
options: It is both O(n) and Ω(n), hence Θ(n)
Ω(n) describes only its best case
O(n²) is false because it is not tight
questions.correct: It is both O(n) and Ω(n), hence Θ(n)
questions.explanation: Bounds apply to the specified runtime function. O(n²) is also a valid loose upper bound; Ω does not change which case is being measured.

questions.title: Output dominates
questions.body: A program returns every permutation of n distinct characters as independent length-n strings. Even if recursion bookkeeping were free, what materialized-output lower bound applies?
options: Ω(n!) only, including all character writes
questions.explanation: There are n! strings of length n. Fixed-word pointer references are not equivalent to independently materialized strings.

questions.title: Repeated letters
questions.body: How many distinct complete strings can be formed by permuting `AABC`?
questions.explanation: Four positions yield 4! index permutations; exchanging the two A positions does not create a new string, so divide by 2!.

questions.title: Unwinding output
questions.body: C++17: `void f(int n){if(n==0)return; f(n-1); cout<<n;}`. What is printed by f(3)?
questions.explanation: The recursive call completes before each print. Stack depth is linear even though output rises from 1 to3.

questions.title: Both sides of the call
questions.body: C++17: `void f(int n){if(n==0)return; cout<<n; f(n-1); cout<<n;}`. What is printed by f(3)?
questions.explanation: Entry prints3,2,1; unwind prints1,2,3. The base call prints nothing.

questions.title: Post-decrement fails progress
questions.body: Java, deliberately faulty: `static int f(int n){if(n==0)return 0;return f(n--);}`. What happens for f(2)?
questions.explanation: Post-decrement passes the old value into the child. The suspended caller decrement does not change the child parameter.

questions.title: Fibonacci call counter
questions.body: Pseudocode: `fib(n): calls++; if n<=1 return n; return fib(n-1)+fib(n-2)`. Starting calls=0, how many invocations for fib(5), including bases?
questions.explanation: C(0)=C(1)=1 and C(n)=1+C(n−1)+C(n−2): C2=3,C3=5,C4=9,C5=15. Sequence value5 is not call count.

questions.title: Time versus active stack
questions.body: For unmemoized fib(n)=fib(n−1)+fib(n−2), n≥2, which pair describes time and stack?
options: Exponential time and exponential simultaneous stack
Θ(n) time and Θ(log n) stack
questions.explanation: Both branches perform work, but they execute at different times; maximum live path has depth n.

questions.title: State recursion
questions.body: Java: `f(n,a,b){if(n==0)return a;return f(n-1,b,a+b);}` with arbitrary-size arithmetic ignored. For f(n,0,1), what is guaranteed?
options: Θ(n) time and Θ(n) call-stack space
Θ(n) time and guaranteed Θ(1) stack
questions.correct: Θ(n) time and Θ(n) call-stack space
questions.explanation: Each call decreases n by1 and does constant bookkeeping. Java does not guarantee tail-call elimination.

questions.title: Ways at zero
questions.body: Counting ordered jumps of length1 or2: ways(n)=ways(n−1)+ways(n−2), ways(0)=1, ways(n<0)=0. What is ways(4)?
questions.explanation: The sequences are1111,112,121,211,22. The empty sequence makes ways(0)=1 and supplies the correct recurrence base.

questions.title: Generalized jumps
questions.body: Ordered jumps1..3 with ways(0)=1 and ways(n<0)=0. What is ways(4)?
questions.explanation: Ways1=1,2=2,3=4; ways4=4+2+1=7. An unordered coin-combination count answers another question.

questions.title: Discarded immutable result
questions.body: Java: `String s="abc"; s.concat("d"); System.out.print(s);` What prints?
questions.explanation: concat returns a new string; the existing immutable object is not changed and the return value is discarded.

questions.title: Shared builder
questions.body: Java: `StringBuilder a=new StringBuilder("ab"); StringBuilder b=a; b.append("c"); System.out.print(a);` What prints?
questions.explanation: Both references point to the same mutable builder. Reassignment of b to a new builder would be a different operation.

questions.title: Reversal recursion space
questions.body: An in-place char-array reversal recursively swaps endpoints then calls reverse(lo+1,hi−1). For length n, absent guaranteed tail-call optimization, what is auxiliary space?
questions.explanation: There are about n/2 nested calls. The array is not duplicated, but the active call frames still consume linear space.

questions.title: Happy-number cycle
questions.body: Repeatedly replace a positive integer by the sum of squared decimal digits. Why is “return false after10 steps” not a correctness criterion?
options: The map must store all integers ever existing
An arbitrary cap lacks a proof; use repeated-state detection or a proven cycle test
questions.correct: An arbitrary cap lacks a proof; use repeated-state detection or a proven cycle test
questions.explanation: The process eventually enters a cycle in a bounded region, but individual steps need not decrease. Visiting1 means happy; repeating another state means unhappy.

questions.title: Signed division
questions.body: Which pair is produced by Java `-3/2` and Python `-3//2`, respectively?
questions.explanation: Java truncates toward zero; Python floor division rounds down. Do not substitute floor for truncation when tracing negative exponents.

questions.title: Hidden copying
questions.body: Python extension: a recurrence makes two recursive calls on copied halves `a[:mid]` and `a[mid:]`, with no other work. What recurrence counts copying at each non-base call?
questions.explanation: Slice construction copies elements proportional to total half lengths. Passing index intervals avoids that copying toll.

questions.title: Exact partition state
questions.body: Last-pivot Lomuto, strict `<`, i=lo; swap passing elements into i then swap a[i],a[hi]. After one partition of [60,50,20,70,30], which result is correct?
questions.explanation: Only20 is smaller than30. Its scan swap precedes the pivot swap; the right side is not yet sorted.

questions.title: Duplicates and strict comparison
questions.body: Same partition on [5,5,5,5] with lo0,hi3. Where is the pivot placed?
questions.explanation: No scanned value is strictly smaller, so i stays0. Equal values move to the right partition and cause a degenerate recursion.

questions.title: Comparison changed
questions.body: Change Lomuto condition to `a[j]<=pivot`, keeping all other rules. On [5,5,5,5], pivot index?
questions.explanation: Every scanned equal value advances i. The degeneration moves to the opposite side; changing equality does not balance all-equal input.

questions.title: Nonshrinking interval
questions.body: Faulty quicksort: after last-pivot partition p, recurse `[lo,p]` and `[p+1,hi]`. Which input can make a branch retain the entire original range?
questions.explanation: Pivot4 is placed at hi; [lo,p] then equals the old interval. For Lomuto, exclude p from both recursive ranges.

questions.title: Linear stack despite in-place
questions.body: Strict last-pivot quicksort runs on an already sorted array of n distinct values. Time and maximum recursive depth?
questions.explanation: Partition sizes repeatedly become n−1 and0. In-place partition does not remove call frames.

questions.title: Randomization guarantee
questions.body: After choosing pivots uniformly at random, which statement is valid for quicksort on distinct keys?
options: Expected Θ(nlogn), but a Θ(n²) worst case remains
questions.correct: Expected Θ(nlogn), but a Θ(n²) worst case remains
questions.explanation: Expected behavior is over pivot choices. Extremely unbalanced choices are still possible; swaps still do not ensure stability.

questions.title: Strict majority
questions.body: For n=6, which minimum frequency satisfies the majority definition?
questions.explanation: A majority exceeds n/2, rather than merely attaining half. n/2 equal-frequency candidates may tie without a majority.

questions.title: Vote counter is not frequency
questions.body: Voting sets candidate when count0, then +1 for match/−1 otherwise. For [1,2,2,2,1,1,1,1,1,2], what are final candidate/count?
questions.explanation: Cancellation discards opposing votes. There are six1s but only a surplus count2 at the end.

questions.title: Missing promise
questions.body: Voting on [1,2,3,4] returns a candidate. What is the necessary final step to support a general majority/no-majority interface?
questions.explanation: Neither a surviving candidate nor a middle sorted element proves existence when the majority promise is absent.

questions.title: D&C complexity
questions.body: D&C majority with index ranges: two half candidates, if unequal count both in the current interval. Worst-case time/stack?
questions.explanation: Linear combining at each of logarithmically many levels gives nlogn. Equality can skip a combine, but that is not the worst-case guarantee.

questions.title: Sentinel collision
questions.body: An implementation uses return−1 to mean no majority, while inputs may contain−1. What makes its interface ambiguous?
options: Negative values can never have majority
questions.explanation: Use optional/status+value. Numeric sentinel choice cannot distinguish this valid answer from absence.

questions.title: Count single-half calls
questions.body: Pseudocode: p(n) counts entry; if n==0 return1; t=p(floor(n/2)); return even? t*t:t*t*x. Calls for n=13, including base?
questions.explanation: Arguments13,6,3,1,0 form five entries. Multiplication values do not add recursive calls.

questions.title: Duplicated half
questions.body: For positive n, code evaluates `power(x,n/2)*power(x,n/2)` as two independent calls at every level. What time bound replaces logarithmic time?
questions.explanation: There are two half-sized calls: T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(1). The active depth is still logarithmic.

questions.title: Widen before negation
questions.body: Java int n=Integer.MIN_VALUE. Which conversion correctly produces its positive magnitude?
questions.explanation: The negation must occur after widening. Negating MIN_VALUE as int wraps to itself; casting afterwards is too late.

questions.title: Integer reciprocal
questions.body: C++17: `int x=2; double y=1/x;` What is y?
questions.explanation: Integer operands perform integer division first; conversion to double occurs after the quotient. Use1.0/x.

questions.title: Negative base
questions.body: A correct single-half power implementation computes power(−2,−3). Result?
questions.explanation: Negative exponent takes the reciprocal; odd exponent preserves negative sign. This is distinct from integer reciprocal truncation.

questions.title: Before final merge
questions.body: Conventional recursive merge sort has finished both child sorts of [6,5,4,3,2,1]. Full array immediately before the top merge?
questions.explanation: The halves are individually sorted and have already been written back. Only the final cross-half merge remains.

questions.title: Inclusive split lengths
questions.body: lo=2,hi=7,mid=lo+(hi−lo)/2=4. Left and right buffer lengths?
questions.explanation: Left includes both endpoints2 and4:3 elements. Right spans5..7:hi−mid=3.

questions.title: Stability on ties
questions.body: Left run records [(2,A),(2,B)], right [(2,C)]. The merge chooses right whenever keys tie. Output label order?
questions.explanation: The right record originally followed the left run but overtakes it. Sorted keys alone do not imply stability.

questions.title: Remaining run
questions.body: Merging [1,4] and [2,3,5], the main two-nonempty loop ends. Which remaining item must be appended?
questions.explanation: Selections1,2,3,4 exhaust the left run. A separate drain handles remaining right items.

questions.title: Sorted input time
questions.body: Unoptimized merge sort always recurses and merges on sorted input of n elements. Tight time?
questions.explanation: Without an explicit already-ordered merge-skip, the same per-level work occurs. Do not transfer quicksort or insertion-sort cases blindly.

questions.title: Peak versus cumulative memory
questions.body: A conventional merge sort allocates merge buffers on demand and releases them when each merge finishes. Which statement can be true?
options: Cumulative allocations equal peak by definition
Peak O(n) live buffer space and Θ(nlogn) cumulative allocated elements
questions.correct: Peak O(n) live buffer space and Θ(nlogn) cumulative allocated elements
questions.explanation: Summing allocations over all levels counts lifetime traffic, not simultaneous memory. Stack adds O(logn).

questions.title: Root-dominated case
questions.body: T(n)=3T(n/2)+Θ(n²), base constant. Tight bound?
questions.explanation: a3 is below b^d=4. Work per level shrinks geometrically relative to root toll.

questions.title: Equal case
questions.body: T(n)=4T(n/2)+Θ(n²). Tight bound?
questions.explanation: Each level contributes Θ(n²) and there are Θ(logn) levels.

questions.title: Leaves dominate
questions.body: T(n)=16T(n/4)+Θ(n). Tight bound?
questions.explanation: log₄16=2 exceeds the toll exponent1. Leaves dominate.

questions.title: Different recurrence family
questions.body: T(n)=T(n−1)+n with T(1)=1. Tight bound and applicable method?
options: Θ(n²), summation rather than this Master-Theorem form
questions.correct: Θ(n²), summation rather than this Master-Theorem form
questions.explanation: There is one subtractively shrinking call. Sum1+2+…+n; no fixed b>1 describes n−1.

questions.title: Level toll
questions.body: For T(n)=3T(n/2)+n², n power of2, what is total nonrecursive work at level i?
questions.explanation: There are3^i subproblems, each toll(n/2^i)². Multiply count by per-node toll.

questions.title: O does not imply tightness
questions.body: Given only T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n), constant base, which conclusion is always supported?
options: T(n)=O(nlogn), but Θ(nlogn) is not established from that toll alone
questions.correct: T(n)=O(nlogn), but Θ(nlogn) is not established from that toll alone
questions.explanation: The actual toll could be constant, giving Θ(n). A tight per-level lower bound is needed for the tight nlogn claim.

questions.title: Pruned ones call count
questions.body: count(lo,hi) counts entry, returns0 if lo>hi or a[hi]==0, returns hi−lo+1 if a[lo]==1, else sequentially calls both halves and sums. For [0,0,0,1,1], count(0,4) entries?
questions.explanation: Root splits0..2 (all0) and3..4 (all1), so two children return immediately.

questions.title: Two calls do not force linear
questions.body: For the pruned sorted0/1 counter above, why is worst-case time O(logn)?
options: It always makes exactly one recursive call
The values are Boolean so recursion is free
At most one child per level still straddles the single0/1 boundary
Every node is pruned at the root
questions.correct: At most one child per level still straddles the single0/1 boundary
questions.explanation: The other child is pure and returns in constant time. Counting syntax instead of surviving subproblems gives the wrong recurrence.

questions.title: Without pruning
questions.body: A count-ones method recursively splits both halves to single elements, without endpoint shortcuts. Time?
questions.explanation: There are n leaves and a linear number of internal nodes. Balanced depth alone does not imply logarithmic total work.

questions.title: Occurrence boundaries
questions.body: For [1,2,2,2,4], first index of2=1,last=3. Which formula counts occurrences?
questions.explanation: Inclusive endpoints require +1. For absent keys, handle the absence sentinel before this formula.

questions.title: First occurrence update
questions.body: Closed-interval binary search on equality records answer=mid. Which update seeks the earliest equal index?
options: hi=mid while lo<=hi without another progress rule
questions.explanation: The equal position is a candidate; any earlier equal must lie left. Using hi=mid with a closed loop can stall.

questions.title: C++ call order
questions.body: C++17: `return traceLeft()+traceRight();` Both functions print their name. What output order is guaranteed by this expression?
options: Neither left-first nor right-first is guaranteed
questions.correct: Neither left-first nor right-first is guaranteed
questions.explanation: Arithmetic operand evaluation order does not enforce a traversal order. Assign sequential temporaries when order is part of the question.

questions.title: Rotation convention
questions.body: Ascending distinct [1,2,3,4,5] becomes [4,5,1,2,3]. Right-rotation count and minimum index?
questions.explanation: Two right rotations put the minimum at2. Three left rotations create the same array but use a different original direction count.

questions.title: Duplicates degrade rotation search
questions.body: An implementation compares a[mid] with a[hi] and on equality executes hi--. Worst-case runtime with duplicates?
questions.explanation: All-equal intervals may shrink only one position at a time; distinctness is necessary for the simple logarithmic guarantee.

questions.title: Fixed point fails with duplicates
questions.body: Faulty fixed-point search uses `if a[mid]<mid: lo=mid+1` on any sorted array. Which input demonstrates losing an existing fixed point?
questions.explanation: At mid2 value0 is smaller, so it discards index0 where a[0]=0. With duplicates a[i]−i need not be nondecreasing.

questions.title: Row counting bug
questions.body: Rows [[2,2],[3,4]]. A hash counter increments per occurrence and declares a value common when count equals row count2. False output?
questions.explanation: Two occurrences from one row imitate presence in two rows. Deduplicate each row or track last row seen.

questions.title: Flattened ordering
questions.body: Rows [1,4,7] and [2,5,8] are individually sorted. Can ordinary binary search on the flattened row-major array be justified?
options: Yes, row sorting implies global ordering
No; the flattened sequence drops from7 to2
Yes, because all values are positive
Only when the target is absent
questions.correct: No; the flattened sequence drops from7 to2
questions.explanation: Row-wise common-element search uses each row separately. Global binary search requires a stronger ordering premise.

questions.title: Exact prefix
questions.body: Longest common prefix of gene, genesis, general?
questions.explanation: All three begin g,e,n,e. The first string then ends, limiting the result to four characters. Trace actual characters rather than accepting a summary correction blindly.

questions.title: Set not cleared
questions.body: For words ["ab","ab"], a set is retained across columns; after inserting each column, code requires set.size()==1. Returned prefix length?
questions.explanation: Column0 leaves {a}; column1 produces {a,b} despite agreement in that column. Clear per-column state.

questions.title: Character work
questions.body: Straightforward binary search on prefix length repeatedly scans prefixes with startsWith. On N identical strings each of length L, character work can be?
questions.explanation: Feasible tested lengths approach L, and each check may read Θ(L) characters over Θ(logL) tests. Monotone feasibility does not make checks constant-time.

questions.title: Java equality
questions.body: Java: `new String("ab")==new String("ab")`. What is the value?
questions.explanation: Two explicit constructions create different objects. Use equals for equal content.

questions.title: Empty member
questions.body: A vertical LCP scan first computes minimum string length. For ["abc",""], what should it return under the normal contract?
questions.explanation: Minimum length0 means no valid common position; guard before indexing.

questions.title: Hours trace
questions.body: At k=22, piles [30,11,23,4,20] need how many total hours?
questions.explanation: Ceilings are2,1,2,1,1. Sum them individually; ceil(total/k) would incorrectly combine piles.

questions.title: First feasible speed
questions.body: Same piles, h=6. Minimum feasible integer speed?
questions.explanation: At22 hours7; at23 hours2+1+1+1+1=6. Monotonicity establishes the first feasible threshold.

questions.title: Predicate direction
questions.body: Binary search minimizes speed. At mid the total hours exceed h. Which update is justified?
questions.explanation: Too many hours means speed too small. Every slower speed is also infeasible.

questions.title: Widening too late
questions.body: Java: `int p=2_000_000_000,k=2_000_000_000; long hours=(p+k-1)/k;` Why is the arithmetic faulty?
options: The int numerator overflows before assignment to long
Division by k is always a floating operation
The long destination prevents any overflow
p itself exceeds Java int range
questions.correct: The int numerator overflows before assignment to long
questions.explanation: Both p and k fit int individually, but their sum does not. Cast p to long before adding; then ceiling is1.

questions.title: Correct search cost
questions.body: n piles, maximum M; each feasibility test scans all piles, binary search over integer speed1..M. Worst-case time?
options: O(nlogn) because piles must be sorted
questions.explanation: Search domain is speed, not indexes; no input sorting is needed.

questions.title: Multiset preserves duplicates
questions.body: Median of sorted arrays [1,2] and [2,3]?
questions.explanation: Merged sequence1,2,2,3 keeps both2s. Deduplicating changes the statistical problem.

questions.title: Integer averaging trap
questions.body: Java/C++ with safe small ints: `(2+3)/2` assigned to double. Value?
questions.explanation: Division is integer before conversion. Use a widened sum divided by2.0.

questions.title: Partition counts
questions.body: A length2, B length5; cut i=1 in A. With leftSize=(m+n+1)/2, what is B cut j?
questions.explanation: LeftSize4 minus cutA1 gives3. Cuts count left elements; they are not element indices.

questions.title: Direction of correction
questions.body: Partition has maxLeftA=9,minRightB=4. How should cutA move?
questions.explanation: Too many large A elements are on the left. Reducing i simultaneously increases B left count.

questions.title: Even partition result
questions.body: A=[1,3],B=[2,4], valid cuts i=1,j=1. Median?
questions.explanation: Left maximum=max(1,2)=2; right minimum=min(3,4)=3. Average them safely.

questions.title: Empty-side boundaries
questions.body: A empty,B=[2,4,6]. Correct odd median partition result?
options: Always reject if either array empty
questions.explanation: Use conceptual infinities for empty A boundaries; B contributes the median. Reject only when both arrays are empty.

questions.title: Smaller-array reason
questions.body: Why swap arrays so partition binary search runs on the smaller one?
options: It reduces search cost and keeps complementary cut within bounds for the usual full search interval
It makes the larger array unsorted
questions.correct: It reduces search cost and keeps complementary cut within bounds for the usual full search interval
questions.explanation: Searching i in0..m with m≤n supports j=(m+n+1)/2−i in0..n. Time is O(log(min(m,n)+1)).

questions.title: Optimal fractional value
questions.body: Items(value,weight)=(60,10),(100,20),(120,30),capacity50. Fractional optimum?
questions.explanation: Take first two fully then20/30 of the third:60+100+80. Taking all three would exceed capacity.

questions.title: Fractions tracked
questions.body: For the same instance, original-order selected fractions?
questions.explanation: Density order6,5,4 fills10+20 first, then remaining20. 0/1 optimum is a different contract.

questions.title: Raw value is insufficient
questions.body: Capacity10, fractional items(value,weight)=(100,100),(60,10). Raw-value descending selects the first fraction. Its value and the density-optimal value?
questions.explanation: First density1 yields10 for10 weight; second density6 yields60. Compare value per unit weight.

questions.title: Integer ratio ties
questions.body: C++ `value/weight` computed as int gives ratios for (5,2) and (7,3). What information is lost?
options: Both truncate to2, hiding the true ordering2.5>7/3
questions.correct: Both truncate to2, hiding the true ordering2.5>7/3
questions.explanation: Floating ratios or safe cross products preserve density order. Tie-breaking among truly equal ratios differs from artificial truncation ties.

questions.title: Why fractional exchange works
questions.body: A solution contains weight from a lower-density item while some higher-density item remains available. With fractions allowed, exchanging equal weights does what?
questions.explanation: Equal-weight exchange preserves capacity and multiplies that weight by a no-smaller density. Indivisible choices may not permit such exchanges.

questions.title: 0/1 has optimal substructure
questions.body: Which statement correctly explains failure of ratio greedy for general0/1 knapsack?
options: The greedy choice can fail even though the problem has optimal substructure
questions.correct: The greedy choice can fail even though the problem has optimal substructure
questions.explanation: An optimal subproblem decomposition is not enough to justify each local greedy decision. Fractional splitting changes what exchanges are allowed.

questions.source: Day 14; activity selection is an extension
questions.title: Class coin counterexample
questions.body: Unlimited coins1,3,4,5, amount7. Greedy count and true minimum count?
questions.explanation: Greedy5+1+1 uses3. Coins3+4 use2, proving largest-first is not generally optimal.

questions.source: Day 14; activity selection is an extension
questions.title: Unreachable remainder
questions.body: Descending coin greedy on [6,4],amount5 uses4. What must the interface acknowledge?
options: Leftover1, so exact change was not produced
One coin is a valid exact answer
Return0 coins because greedy is always optimal
questions.correct: Leftover1, so exact change was not produced
questions.explanation: Allowed denominations contain no1. A greedy decomposition may leave remainder; exact-change feasibility needs its own treatment.

questions.source: Day 14; activity selection is an extension
questions.title: Coin output cost
questions.body: For amountA, k denominations, compare repeated coin output with counts `(denomination,count)`.
options: Counts require more than A records
Counts avoid Θ(A) output when denomination1 supplies the amount
questions.correct: Counts avoid Θ(A) output when denomination1 supplies the amount
questions.explanation: A literal list of A ones has unavoidable Θ(A) size. Count representation uses at most k records; optimality is a separate issue.

questions.source: Day 14; activity selection is an extension
questions.title: Activity selection trace
questions.body: Half-open intervals [1,3),[2,4),[3,5),[0,6),[5,7). Earliest-finish greedy selects how many?
questions.explanation: Select[1,3),[3,5),[5,7). Equality of next start with last finish is compatible under this contract.

questions.source: Day 14; activity selection is an extension
questions.title: Wrong greedy criterion
questions.body: Intervals [0,10),[1,2),[2,3),[3,4). Earliest-start-first accepts0..10. Maximum compatible count?
questions.explanation: The three short intervals chain and are compatible. Earliest finish has the exchange property; earliest start alone does not.

questions.title: Neighbour scan
questions.body: A graph has V vertices and adjacency matrix. Enumerating all neighbours of a given vertex costs?
questions.explanation: O(1) edge lookup does not mean O(1) enumeration. An adjacency list directly stores present neighbours.

questions.title: Undirected list storage
questions.body: An ordinary adjacency list represents an undirected graph with V vertices,E edges, storing each edge at both endpoints. Space?
questions.explanation: There are V list heads and2E neighbour records; a constant factor2 does not change asymptotic order.

questions.title: Zero ambiguity
questions.body: A weighted matrix uses0 to mean no edge. What valid Dijkstra-compatible feature can it fail to represent?
questions.explanation: Dijkstra accepts nonnegative weights. Separate existence from weight so zero is not overloaded.

questions.title: Directed matrix
questions.body: Matrix entries w[0][1]=5,w[1][0]=0 where0 means absence. What can be inferred?
options: A directed edge0→1 need not have the reverse edge
A symmetric matrix is compulsory for every graph
No graph can have this matrix
questions.correct: A directed edge0→1 need not have the reverse edge
questions.explanation: Symmetry is an undirected representation condition, not a universal graph rule.

questions.title: Relaxation arithmetic
questions.body: dist[u]=5,weight(u,v)=6,current dist[v]=12. Correct new tentative distance?
questions.explanation: Relax using the source distance5 plus edge6, then compare11 with12. Edge weight alone is Prim-style information.

questions.title: Next finite vertex
questions.body: Tentative distances[5,12,0,∞,∞], vertex2 already visited. Which unvisited vertex is chosen next?
questions.explanation: Vertex0 has smallest remaining finite distance5. Do not confuse a vertex label with its distance.

questions.title: Matrix runtime
questions.body: Dijkstra selects minimum unvisited distance by scanning V entries, then scans a V-entry row, for up to V vertices. Time?
questions.explanation: Two linear scans per outer iteration remain O(V), yielding O(V²), not a product of three nested V loops.

questions.title: Nonnegative requirement
questions.body: Which weight restriction is sufficient for standard Dijkstra correctness?
options: All edges nonnegative; zero is allowed
Any weights if no negative cycle
Negative undirected edges are always fine
questions.correct: All edges nonnegative; zero is allowed
questions.explanation: Negative edges can improve an already-finalized vertex. A zero-weight edge is harmless when represented properly.

questions.title: Counterexample with negative edge
questions.body: Directed edges s→a:2,s→b:5,b→a:−4. Dijkstra finalizes a before b. True shortest s→a?
options: 1, so finalizing2 without revisits is wrong
There must be a negative cycle
questions.correct: 1, so finalizing2 without revisits is wrong
questions.explanation: s→b→a costs1. There is no directed cycle here, but the negative edge still breaks the finalization proof.

questions.title: Disconnected case
questions.body: All remaining unvisited distances are∞. A matrix implementation has no finite chosen index. What should it do?
options: Stop/reject unreachable vertices rather than index with an invalid choice
questions.correct: Stop/reject unreachable vertices rather than index with an invalid choice
questions.explanation: Unreachable vertices stay∞. Guard before accessing a row or performing finite-distance arithmetic.

questions.title: One versus unlimited
questions.body: prices=[7,1,5,3,6,4], no fee/cooldown. One-transaction and unlimited maximum profits?
questions.explanation: One buy1/sell6 gives5. Unlimited gains(5−1)+(6−3)=7. Same array, different feasible actions.

questions.title: Update invariant
questions.body: One-transaction scan has minPrice=1,best=4 before price3. After processing3, state?
questions.explanation: Minimum earlier price stays1; current possible profit2 does not replace the larger previous best4.

questions.title: Declining market
questions.body: prices=[9,7,4,1], at most one buy/sell and doing nothing allowed. Profit?
questions.explanation: No positive later-price difference exists. Initial best0 represents choosing no transaction.

questions.title: Summing rises
questions.body: Unlimited prices=[1,2,2,5,3,4]. Sum of positive adjacent differences?
questions.explanation: Gains1+0+3+0+1=5. A zero change neither helps nor hurts.

questions.title: Fee extension invalidates formula
questions.body: Extension: prices=[1,3], fee1 per completed transaction. Plain sum-positive-differences returns2. Correct net profit?
questions.explanation: The single gain2 incurs fee1. The no-fee greedy formula is not automatically correct after changing the contract.

questions.title: Even negatives
questions.body: Minimum nonempty subset product of [−2,−3,4]?
questions.explanation: All nonzeros product24; drop closest-to-zero negative−2 to get−12. Dropping−3 gives−8, which is larger.

questions.title: Zeros do not force zero
questions.body: Minimum subset product of [−1,0]?
questions.explanation: A singleton−1 is allowed and is less than zero. Including every array element is not required.

questions.title: All positives
questions.body: Minimum nonempty subset product of integer values[2,3,5]?
questions.explanation: No empty subset is allowed; every product of multiple integers≥1 cannot beat the smallest value2.

questions.title: Even negative units
questions.body: Minimum nonempty subset product of [−1,−1]?
questions.explanation: A single−1 yields the negative minimum; selecting both gives+1. Even-negative handling must permit dropping one.

questions.title: Integers are an assumption
questions.body: Extension: apply “multiply all nonzeros with odd negative count” to real values[−10,0.2]. It returns−2. True minimum nonempty subset product?
questions.explanation: Positive values below1 shrink negative magnitude. The class greedy rule is justified for integer inputs, not arbitrary real values.

questions.title: Tie chooses rightmost
questions.body: At most one swap on1993. Largest result?
questions.explanation: Swap first1 with the later9. 9931 would require additional rearrangement; the rightmost maximum preserves a larger earlier suffix.

questions.title: Suffix maximum indexes
questions.body: For digits84725, rightmost suffix-maximum indices for each position?
questions.explanation: From right:5 at4 dominates2;7 at2 dominates5;4 points to2;8 at0 dominates all. These are indexes, not digit values.

questions.title: Only one exchange
questions.body: Maximum Swap result for84725?
questions.explanation: First improvable position is digit4, suffix maximum7. Swap these and stop; sorting all digits violates the at-most-one-swap rule.

questions.title: Equal maximum update
questions.body: Scanning suffixes right-to-left, new digit equals currently tracked maximum. To retain rightmost tie, should the index update?
options: No; update only on strictly larger digit
questions.correct: No; update only on strictly larger digit
questions.explanation: The existing maximum is farther right. Keeping it makes the eventual displaced smaller digit land later.

questions.title: Edge count
questions.body: An undirected connected graph has6 vertices. Any spanning tree contains how many edges?
questions.explanation: Connected acyclic graphs have V−1 edges. Weight values affect optimum choice, not spanning-tree edge count.

questions.title: Keys differ from distances
questions.body: Prim key[u]=4,edge(u,v)=3,current key[v]=5. Correct updated key[v]?
questions.explanation: Prim compares the single edge crossing the cut. Adding key[u] would confuse it with source-distance relaxation.

questions.title: Objective contrast
questions.body: Triangle edges0–1:2,1–2:2,0–2:3. MST edges versus source0 shortest-path tree?
options: MST requires edge3 because it is direct
MST uses2+2; shortest-path tree uses edges2 and3
questions.correct: MST uses2+2; shortest-path tree uses edges2 and3
questions.explanation: MST total4 via chain, but direct0→2 costs3 versus chain4. Global edge sum differs from individual path distance.

questions.title: Negative weights in MST
questions.body: Connected undirected graph has some negative edge weights. What about MST algorithms Prim/Kruskal?
options: They require nonnegative edges like Dijkstra
Negative weights are allowed for the MST objective
They must reject all negative graphs
A negative edge makes spanning trees undefined
questions.correct: Negative weights are allowed for the MST objective
questions.explanation: A finite set of spanning trees still has a minimum sum. MST never repeats edges around a negative cycle.

questions.title: Disconnected Prim
questions.body: Prim from vertex0 exhausts all finite keys while some vertices remain unselected. What is indicated?
options: Graph disconnected; no spanning tree over all vertices
An MST already spans all vertices
The key array must be reset to zero
Every remaining vertex is a leaf of the same tree
questions.correct: Graph disconnected; no spanning tree over all vertices
questions.explanation: A minimum spanning forest can be computed deliberately, but a single connected spanning tree does not exist.

questions.title: Root differs from direct parent
questions.body: parent=[0,0,1,3]. find(2) follows parents recursively. Returned representative?
questions.explanation: 2→1→0. parent[2] by itself is not necessarily the component representative.

questions.title: Path compression write
questions.body: Same parent array, after compressed find(2), what becomes parent[2]?
questions.explanation: Assign the root to each visited node on unwind. This changes tree shape, not component membership.

questions.title: Attach roots only
questions.body: parent=[0,0,2,2]. To unite components containing1 and3, which conceptual action is correct?
options: Set parent[1]=3 only; all of component0 must move automatically
Find roots0 and2 and link one root under the other
Set parent[0]=1 to create a cycle
Change rank without changing any parent
questions.correct: Find roots0 and2 and link one root under the other
questions.explanation: Reparenting an arbitrary child can split rather than merge components. Union operates on representatives.

questions.title: Unequal-rank union
questions.body: Roots a,b have ranks3,1. Standard union-by-rank attaches b below a. New rank[a]?
questions.explanation: Only equal-rank merges increase rank. Attaching a lower-height upper-bound tree does not force the root height to grow.

questions.title: Equal ranks
questions.body: Two different roots both rank2 are united under one chosen root. New rank of chosen root?
questions.explanation: Equal-height upper bounds may add one level, so increment by1. The losing root rank is no longer used as a root heuristic.

questions.title: Amortized is not per-call constant
questions.body: With union by rank and path compression, standard bound for a long operation sequence?
options: Every individual find is worst-case O(1)
Path compression removes the need to follow parents ever
questions.explanation: The inverse-Ackermann bound describes amortized work. A particular initial find can still traverse multiple links.

questions.title: Cycle test
questions.body: Accepted edges0–1 and1–2. Candidate edge0–2. DSU roots of0 and2 agree. Action?
options: Accept because direct parents might differ
Reject it as forming a cycle
questions.correct: Reject it as forming a cycle
questions.explanation: Root equality means there is already a path between endpoints in the accepted forest.

questions.title: Acceptance count
questions.body: V=4, sorted edges(0,1,1),(1,2,2),(0,2,3),(2,3,4). MST total weight?
questions.explanation: Accept1,2; reject3 as cycle; accept4. Need three accepted edges, not merely three examined edges.

questions.title: Necessary not sufficient
questions.body: V=4,E=3 with triangle0–1,1–2,2–0 and isolated3. Does E≥V−1 prove connectivity?
options: Only if weights positive, then yes
A triangle automatically covers all vertices
questions.explanation: Edge count alone cannot show all vertices are connected. A disconnected graph can have many edges.

questions.title: Exhausted list
questions.body: Kruskal loops until accepted=V−1 but never checks nextIndex<E. On a disconnected graph, likely code failure?
options: It correctly returns an MST every time
It must find a new edge automatically
It always terminates after exactly V−1 reads
questions.explanation: The Day18 demonstration reaches this failure. Guard edge exhaustion and report a forest/no full spanning tree.

questions.title: Comparator overflow
questions.body: Java comparator returns `a.weight-b.weight`. For a.weight=2_000_000_000,b.weight=−2_000_000_000, what is the defect?
options: Both weights individually exceed int range
Subtraction overflows int and can reverse ordering
Comparison returns only0 or1 by language rule
questions.correct: Subtraction overflows int and can reverse ordering
questions.explanation: Use Integer.compare/Long.compare or a suitable comparison. MST correctness depends on actual ascending weights.

questions.title: BFS order specified
questions.body: Graph adjacency in ascending order:0:[1,2],1:[0,3],2:[0,3],3:[1,2]. BFS from0 marks on enqueue. Dequeue order?
questions.explanation: FIFO processes all depth1 vertices before depth2. Node3 is enqueued once when first discovered.

questions.title: Marking too late
questions.body: Same graph, visited only when dequeued and no pending-state check. What can happen before3 is dequeued?
questions.explanation: 3 is still unvisited when2 examines it. Marking on enqueue prevents the duplicate pending copy.

questions.title: Shortest-path condition
questions.body: BFS first-discovery depth minimizes what in an unweighted graph?
options: Number of edges from the source
questions.correct: Number of edges from the source
questions.explanation: Each queue layer adds one edge. Weighted paths need a matching algorithm/objective.

questions.title: Source coverage
questions.body: BFS starts in one component of a disconnected graph. What is needed to visit every vertex?
options: The first queue eventually jumps components
Start additional traversals from remaining unvisited vertices
Add all edges to a stack
questions.correct: Start additional traversals from remaining unvisited vertices
questions.explanation: No edge reaches another component. A traversal loop over vertices covers them independently.

questions.title: FIFO versus LIFO
questions.body: BFS-like code uses push_back and pop_back from the same sequence rather than removing the front. What changes?
options: It uses LIFO exploration, so BFS level-order guarantees no longer apply
questions.correct: It uses LIFO exploration, so BFS level-order guarantees no longer apply
questions.explanation: Queue discipline is the reason BFS processes layers. A stack changes pending-state order.

questions.title: Root is excluded
questions.body: Tree root1 has only left child2; node2 has children3 and4. Lonely node values?
questions.explanation: 2 lacks a sibling. Root has no parent and is excluded; children3 and4 are siblings.

questions.title: Leaf does not imply lonely
questions.body: A parent has two leaf children7 and8. Which are lonely?
questions.explanation: Loneliness depends on whether a sibling exists, not whether the node itself has children.

questions.title: Condition implements XOR
questions.body: Which parent test correctly identifies exactly one child?
questions.explanation: Boolean inequality is exclusive-or of absence. Avoid dereferencing missing children while testing.

questions.title: Diagonal separation
questions.body: Grid [[1,0],[0,1]], four-neighbour land. Island count and max area?
questions.explanation: Diagonal contact is not a permitted edge. Each component has one cell.

questions.title: Three objectives
questions.body: Grid [[1,1,0,1],[0,0,0,0],[1,1,0,1]]. Four-neighbour components. Count,max area,distinct translation-only shapes?
questions.explanation: Two horizontal dominoes and two singles form four components, maximum2 and two distinct shapes.

questions.title: Area not shape
questions.body: Two islands each have3 cells: a horizontal line and an L. Can area alone deduplicate their shapes?
options: Yes, by definition of distinct islands
No; equal area can have different arrangements
Every3-cell island is equivalent by translation
questions.correct: No; equal area can have different arrangements
questions.explanation: Translations preserve relative positions. A line cannot become an L by translation.

questions.title: Signature reliability
questions.body: Shape serialization records only successful DFS direction letters, dropping returns/null transitions. Why is a structural marker or coordinate canonicalization safer?
options: String sets cannot store equal strings
Different branch structures can lose distinctions in a bare move sequence
questions.correct: Different branch structures can lose distinctions in a bare move sequence
questions.explanation: Record enough structure to reconstruct positions. Fixed-order relative coordinate sets are a clear translation-invariant contract.

questions.title: Destructive marking reused
questions.body: An island counter turns visited1s into0. Run it twice on the same grid without copying/resetting. Second result?
questions.explanation: The first traversal has consumed all land. State ownership matters when comparing methods on one input.

questions.title: Grid complexity
questions.body: Each land cell is enqueued at most once; four neighbours examined. Full grid dimensions R,C. Time and worst-case queue/visited storage?
options: O(RC) time and always O(1) queue
questions.explanation: The constant four-direction loop does not add an asymptotic factor. Large components can require linear state.

questions.section: DFS and the actual class maze
questions.title: Push order
questions.body: Tree root1,left2,right3. Iterative preorder should visit left before right. Which stack push order after popping1?
questions.explanation: LIFO visits the last pushed item first. This simple tree avoids extra graph discovery-order complications.

questions.section: DFS and the actual class maze
questions.title: Maze contract
questions.body: Which moves are permitted in the Day21–22 class rat maze?
options: Roll in all directions until a wall
questions.explanation: Day22 opening explicitly says1 is open,0 blocked, right and down. Do not map a title to a different LeetCode state transition.

questions.section: DFS and the actual class maze
questions.title: Maze reachability
questions.body: Class maze [[1,1,0],[0,1,1],[0,0,1]], start(0,0),end(2,2). Reachable?
options: No because down from start is blocked
No because maze must be symmetric
questions.explanation: An invalid first direction should allow the other direction. Reachability does not require every adjacent cell to be open.

questions.section: DFS and the actual class maze
questions.title: Bounds before access
questions.body: C++ deliberately faulty: `if(grid[r][c]==0 || r>=R || c>=C)return false;` Called with r=R. What is wrong?
options: It safely returns false by short-circuit
It accesses out-of-bounds before checking bounds: undefined behavior
questions.correct: It accesses out-of-bounds before checking bounds: undefined behavior
questions.explanation: Short-circuit checks left first. Put bounds tests before indexing; vector operator[] is unchecked.

questions.section: DFS and the actual class maze
questions.title: No cycles does not eliminate repeats
questions.body: Right/down recursive reachability has no visited/memoization and explores both branches on a no-path grid. Which can occur?
options: No repeated subproblem because no cycles
The same cell is recomputed through multiple routes, causing exponential worst-case work
questions.correct: The same cell is recomputed through multiple routes, causing exponential worst-case work
questions.explanation: r+c strictly increases, so recursion terminates. Different paths still merge at cells; memoized reachability is O(RC).

questions.section: DFS and the actual class maze
questions.title: One-cell maze
questions.body: Class maze [[1]], start and destination both(0,0). Correct reachability?
options: false because no move is possible
true even if its only value were0
questions.explanation: Start is already the open destination. Check cell validity before treating that destination match as success.

questions.title: Boundary order
questions.body: Tree1 with left2,right3;2 has leaves4,5;3 has leaves6,7. Anticlockwise boundary without duplicates?
questions.explanation: Root; nonleaf left boundary; all leaves left-to-right; reversed nonleaf right boundary.

questions.title: Singleton tree
questions.body: Boundary of a single-node tree9?
questions.explanation: Root is also a leaf. Avoid adding it independently in multiple boundary phases.

questions.title: Left fallback
questions.body: While collecting nonleaf left boundary, current node has no left child but has a right child. Next step?
options: Visit both children as left-boundary nodes
questions.explanation: The boundary follows the available exterior route. Leaves will be handled separately.

questions.title: Right side reversal
questions.body: Right boundary top-down is3,8,10 excluding leaves. What order is appended at the end of anticlockwise boundary?
questions.explanation: The final traversal climbs from the leaves back toward the root, so this side must reverse.

questions.title: Height convention
questions.body: Node-height definition h(null)=0,h(node)=1+max(children). Height of a3-node chain?
questions.explanation: Edge-height would be2. Use the exact base convention; balance differences remain the same if consistent.

questions.title: Mirror arguments
questions.body: isMirror(a,b) finds equal values. Which recursive pairings are required?
questions.explanation: Reflection reverses child directions. Equal shape without reflection is the same-tree problem.

questions.title: Exactly one null
questions.body: isMirror receives a=null,b=non-null. Correct result?
questions.explanation: Missingness is part of structure; guard before dereferencing.

questions.title: Same values, wrong placement
questions.body: Root1 has left2 with left child3, and right2 also with left child3. Symmetric?
questions.explanation: The right-side3 would need to be a right child. Omitting null placeholders from level sequences can hide this mismatch.

questions.title: Root test is insufficient
questions.body: Root has two equal-height children, but one subtree has a node with child-height difference2. Is the whole tree balanced?
options: No; every node must meet the bound
Yes if total node count is odd
questions.correct: No; every node must meet the bound
questions.explanation: Local height balance is required recursively; root-only checking loses violations below it.

questions.title: Sentinel propagation
questions.body: One-pass check returns−1 for an unbalanced subtree; left=−1,right=2. Correct next action?
options: Return abs(left−right)=3 as a valid height
Return−1 before using them as heights
questions.correct: Return−1 before using them as heights
questions.explanation: Here normal null height is0, so−1 is reserved error state. Propagate it instead of masking an earlier imbalance.

questions.title: One-pass height result
questions.body: Balanced node has child heights2 and3, node-height convention. Returned height?
questions.explanation: Difference1 passes; one plus maximum3 gives4. Balance is not a sum of child heights.

questions.title: Repeated heights
questions.body: Naive balance recomputes height(left/right) at every node of a long skewed tree. Worst-case time?
questions.explanation: Subtree scans have sizes n−1,n−2,… . One postorder computes each height once.

questions.title: Counts are not heights
questions.body: Two child subtrees have equal numbers of nodes but one is a chain and the other compact. Does equality of counts guarantee local height balance?
options: Only if root has two children, then yes
questions.explanation: Structural depth, not cardinality, defines height. Equal cardinality can support different heights.

questions.title: Correct averages
questions.body: Tree3 has children9,20;20 has children15,7. Per-level averages?
questions.explanation: Levels are[3],[9,20],[15,7]. Floating division preserves the half unit.

questions.title: Snapshot size
questions.body: BFS level loop pushes children. Why capture n=q.size() before entering that level loop?
options: To prevent any children being visited ever
To process exactly the current level despite the queue growing/shrinking
questions.correct: To process exactly the current level despite the queue growing/shrinking
questions.explanation: Using a changing queue size as the loop bound can mix levels or stop too early. Level membership is defined at entry.

questions.title: Overflow before average
questions.body: Java int sum adds two level values2_000_000_000,then divides by2.0. What prevents overflow?
options: Only cast the final sum to double
Use a long accumulator before additions
Division by2.0 retroactively widens earlier additions
questions.correct: Use a long accumulator before additions
questions.explanation: Overflow occurs while summing int values. Later floating conversion cannot reconstruct the intended sum.

questions.title: DFS missing state
questions.body: A DFS records only sum[depth]. To compute level averages later, what else is needed?
options: A single global count for the whole tree
questions.explanation: Each depth can contain different numbers of nodes. Divide its own sum by its own count.

questions.title: Traversal order versus aggregate
questions.body: DFS with explicit depth and BFS with level snapshots both correctly accumulate sums/counts. Can final level averages agree despite different visitation order?
options: No; DFS can never group levels
Only if all values are equal
questions.explanation: Grouping by depth determines the aggregate, not the order of visits, provided arithmetic and state are correct.

questions.title: Undo the choice
questions.body: A used-array permutation search sets used[i]=true, recurses, but never restores it. Effect on sibling branches?
options: It necessarily enumerates all permutations twice
No effect because recursion copies shared arrays automatically
Legal choices can be incorrectly unavailable
It improves correctness by remembering all explored paths
questions.correct: Legal choices can be incorrectly unavailable
questions.explanation: Used flags represent the current path, not every historical choice. Undo when returning to a sibling.

questions.title: Copied output
questions.body: Java recursion appends the same mutable path list object at every leaf, then pops elements. What can fix corrupted stored outputs?
options: Store a new copy at each leaf
questions.correct: Store a new copy at each leaf
questions.explanation: Stored references share later mutations. Snapshotting preserves each completed choice sequence.

questions.title: Queen diagonal test
questions.body: Queens at(r1,c1) and(r2,c2), distinct rows. Diagonal attack condition?
questions.explanation: Same r−c or r+c identifies the two diagonal directions. Column equality is a separate conflict.

questions.title: Four queens count
questions.body: Enumerating all standard N-Queens placements for n=4, one queen per row/column. Total solutions?
questions.explanation: Column sequences[1,3,0,2] and[2,0,3,1] are the two placements. Finding the first one is not enumerating both.

questions.title: Five queens count
questions.body: Enumerating all standard N-Queens placements for n=5. Total solutions?
questions.explanation: A lecturer demonstrating two possibilities does not establish completeness. Exhaustive row/column/diagonal search yields10.

questions.title: Search bound assumptions
questions.body: Place one queen per row, never reuse a column, check conflicts using O(1) sets. Useful upper bound on search states excluding output-board copying?
questions.explanation: Column-unique branches form partial permutations; diagonals prune them. Scanning board cells or emitting boards adds its own work.

questions.title: Component sum is not path sum
questions.body: Plus-shaped grid [[0,1,0],[1,1,1],[0,1,0]], four directions, no cell revisited. Maximum gold path sum?
questions.explanation: A path can enter the centre from one arm and leave to one other arm; taking a third arm would require revisiting the centre. Component area/sum5 is not achievable.

questions.title: Restore after recursion
questions.body: Gold search marks grid[r][c]=0 before exploring. Why restore the saved value on return?
options: To allow revisiting within the same path
Because zeros count as extra gold
Because BFS needs a sorted grid
Other candidate paths/start cells may legally use that cell later
questions.correct: Other candidate paths/start cells may legally use that cell later
questions.explanation: Temporary marking forbids use in the current path. Permanent global consumption wrongly blocks independent paths.

questions.title: Simple gold trace
questions.body: Grid [[0,6,0],[5,8,7],[0,9,0]]. Maximum gold without revisits?
questions.explanation: Path7→8→9 gives24. Summing all arms requires revisiting8;6→8→9 gives23.

questions.title: Start coverage
questions.body: Gold path may start anywhere. Which outer search is necessary?
options: Try every positive cell as a start, preserving input between tries
Only start at maximum-valued cell by greedy guarantee
Skip all cells with one neighbour
questions.correct: Try every positive cell as a start, preserving input between tries
questions.explanation: An optimal path endpoint need not be the largest cell or top-left. Greedy start choice is not proved by the problem definition.

questions.title: Closing edge
questions.body: A path contains every vertex once, but last vertex has no edge back to first. Is it a Hamiltonian cycle?
options: No; it may be a Hamiltonian path only
Yes if last value is largest
questions.correct: No; it may be a Hamiltonian path only
questions.explanation: The base case must check the closing adjacency, not simply path lengthV.

questions.title: Repeated vertex
questions.body: Candidate path0,1,2,1,3,0 in a4-vertex graph. What violates Hamiltonian-cycle rules?
options: Returning to0 at end is always forbidden
Any cycle must use exactly one edge
questions.explanation: Start repeats only as final closure; all other vertices occur once. Edges alone cannot validate this vertex sequence.

questions.title: Vertices versus edges
questions.body: What is the essential distinction between Hamiltonian and Eulerian cycles?
options: Both optimize total weight by definition
Hamiltonian visits vertices once; Eulerian traverses edges once
Eulerian requires every vertex once only
questions.correct: Hamiltonian visits vertices once; Eulerian traverses edges once
questions.explanation: A connected graph can satisfy one property without the other. Neither name alone states weighted shortest-tour optimization.

questions.title: Any cycle versus best tour
questions.body: Finding the first Hamiltonian cycle in a weighted graph does what for TSP?
options: Shows a feasible tour, not necessarily the minimum-weight tour
questions.correct: Shows a feasible tour, not necessarily the minimum-weight tour
questions.explanation: Existence and optimization are different goals; more expensive valid cycles can be found first.

questions.title: Fixing the start
questions.body: When enumerating undirected Hamiltonian cycles, fixing start vertex0 removes what redundancy?
options: Cyclic rotations of a tour; reverse-direction duplication may remain
questions.correct: Cyclic rotations of a tour; reverse-direction duplication may remain
questions.explanation: A reversed cycle may still be enumerated with the same start. Canonical orientation is an additional convention.

questions.title: Cartesian output
questions.body: Expand {a,b}{c,d} under set grammar. Sorted output?
questions.explanation: Concatenation chooses one member of each set. Commas inside braces form alternatives, not concatenated strings.

questions.title: Nested union
questions.body: Expand {a,{b,c}}d. Sorted output?
questions.explanation: Nested alternatives flatten by union; each selected word concatenates with d.

questions.title: Deduplication
questions.body: Expand {{a,b},{b,c}}. Sorted unique output?
questions.explanation: The grammar denotes sets, so repeated b is present once. Sorting alone does not remove duplicates.

questions.title: Wrong delimiter match
questions.body: A parser pairs first opening brace with the first following closing brace regardless of depth. Why does {a,{b,c}} fail?
options: That first closing brace belongs to the inner group
All braces must be flat by this contract
questions.correct: That first closing brace belongs to the inner group
questions.explanation: Track nesting depth or use recursive parsing; only depth-zero separators split the current union.

questions.title: Output-size lower bound
questions.body: Flat groups each choose a or b at n positions, return all length-n strings. Minimum materialization cost?
options: O(n) because parser reads n groups
questions.explanation: Parsing can be linear in input while expanded output is exponential. Complexity must include generated words.

questions.title: Reflected three-bit sequence
questions.body: Using g(i)=i^(i>>1),i0..7. Sequence?
questions.explanation: XOR each binary index with its right-shifted value. Consecutive binary increments become single Gray-bit changes.

questions.title: XOR neighbour
questions.body: Current x=3(binary011); toggle bit1 with x^(1<<1). New value?
questions.explanation: 011 XOR010=001. OR would keep an already-set bit unchanged.

questions.title: Closing pair
questions.body: Candidate n2 sequence[0,1,3,2]. Last-to-first XOR?
questions.explanation: 2 XOR0=2(binary10). The cyclic Gray contract checks closure as well as internal pairs.

questions.title: Duplicate state
questions.body: A sequence toggles one bit each step but revisits an earlier integer. Is it a complete valid n-bit Gray sequence?
